name: Part 3 — Practice
tagline: Abstract questions, four minutes, and an examiner who will push back
blurb: The full Quarter 3 discussion bank sorted by theme, the argumentative language it calls for, the structures that carry reasoning, and three model answers to compare against — after you have recorded your own.
modelQ: Why do some people find it difficult to make important decisions?
modelType: The CAUSE type — obvious reason dispatched, less obvious reason developed, then ranked.

items: a generation gap
noun phrase
/ˌdʒenəˈreɪʃn ɡæp/
Difference in outlook between age groups.
There's a genuine generation gap here, though it's about how people communicate rather than what they believe.
by and large
phrase
/baɪ ən ˈlɑːdʒ/
Broadly true, exceptions acknowledged. The safest generalising hedge.
By and large people are more environmentally conscious than they were, though awareness and behaviour are different things.
set in their ways
idiom
/set ɪn ðeə ˈweɪz/
Resistant to change through long habit.
It isn't that older people are set in their ways; it's that they've seen more things fail.
come round to
phrasal verb
/kʌm ˈraʊnd tə/
Gradually accept an idea previously rejected.
Most people come round to it eventually, but it takes a decade rather than a campaign.
the pendulum has swung
idiom
/ˈpendjʊləm/
Opinion has moved decisively the other way.
The pendulum has swung so far towards flexibility that some companies are now swinging back.
cut both ways
idiom
/kʌt bəʊθ ˈweɪz/
Have consequences in both directions.
That cuts both ways, though — the same openness that connects people also exposes them.
an echo chamber
noun phrase
/ˈekəʊ ˌtʃeɪmbə/
An environment offering only agreeing opinions.
The algorithm builds an echo chamber around you quietly enough that you never notice it happening.
at the expense of
phrase
/ɪkˈspens/
With a cost to something else.
We've gained enormous convenience at the expense of ever being genuinely unreachable.
blur the line between
collocation
/blɜː/
Make a distinction harder to see.
Social media has blurred the line between reporting something and simply having an opinion about it.
a double-edged sword
idiom
/ˈsɔːd/
Brings costs alongside benefits. The w is silent.
Remote learning is a double-edged sword: it widens access and isolates exactly the students who need contact.
take with a pinch of salt
idiom
/pɪntʃ/
Treat with reasonable scepticism.
I'd take any figure that's trending online with a pinch of salt until a proper outlet confirms it.
level the playing field
idiom
/ˈleɪvl/
Make competition fairer.
Free online courses have levelled the playing field a little, though not nearly as much as people claim.
a deterrent
noun
/dɪˈterənt/
Something that discourages an action. Central to punishment questions.
A fine only works as a deterrent if it's large enough to be inconvenient to people who can afford it.
at the point of sale
phrase
/pɔɪnt əv ˈseɪl/
At the moment of purchase. Precise and policy-flavoured.
A levy at the point of sale changes behaviour because it arrives at the moment the decision is made.
the lion's share
idiom
/ˈlaɪənz ʃeə/
The largest part by far.
Industry produces the lion's share of the emissions, so asking households to do more is largely symbolic.
pay lip service to
idiom
/lɪp ˈsɜːvɪs/
Express support without acting on it.
A lot of companies pay lip service to sustainability and change nothing that costs them money.
in the long run
phrase
/lɒŋ rʌn/
Over an extended period. Pairs with a short-run contrast.
It's more expensive initially, but in the long run it's considerably cheaper than the alternative.
shift the burden onto
collocation
/ˈbɜːdn/
Move responsibility to someone else.
Recycling campaigns quietly shift the burden onto consumers for a problem manufacturers created.
well-rounded
adjective
/wel ˈraʊndɪd/
Competent across many areas.
Schools say they want well-rounded students and then rank them on two subjects.
play to your strengths
idiom
/streŋθs/
Concentrate on what you are already good at.
There's a real argument for letting children play to their strengths rather than fixing every weakness.
a head start
noun phrase
/hed ˈstɑːt/
An early advantage.
Starting a language at five gives a child a head start that's very hard to close later.
rote learning
noun phrase
/rəʊt/
Memorisation without understanding.
Rote learning gets you through an exam and abandons you the week afterwards.
bring out the best in
collocation
/brɪŋ ˈaʊt/
Cause someone to perform at their highest level.
A good teacher brings out the best in the students nobody else had noticed.
nature versus nurture
phrase
/ˈneɪtʃə ˈnɜːtʃə/
The innate-versus-learned debate. Names the question directly.
It's the old nature-versus-nurture question, and my sense is that environment does far more of the work.
live within your means
idiom
/wɪˈðɪn jɔː ˈmiːnz/
Spend no more than you earn.
Learning to live within your means is a skill, and nobody is taught it anywhere.
instant gratification
noun phrase
/ˌɡrætɪfɪˈkeɪʃn/
The desire for immediate reward.
Everything is now engineered around instant gratification, which makes saving feel like a punishment.
a false economy
noun phrase
/fɔːls ɪˈkɒnəmi/
An apparent saving that costs more later.
Buying the cheapest version is usually a false economy — you replace it twice and pay more overall.
price somebody out of
phrasal verb
/praɪs ˈaʊt/
Make something unaffordable for a group.
Rising rents have priced young people out of the areas they grew up in.
disposable income
noun phrase
/dɪˈspəʊzəbl/
Money left after essentials are paid for.
Young people have more disposable income than their parents did and considerably less security.
keep up with the Joneses
idiom
/ˈdʒəʊnzɪz/
Compete socially through spending.
A lot of spending isn't about wanting the thing; it's about keeping up with the Joneses.
a stepping stone
noun phrase
/ˈstepɪŋ stəʊn/
A position that leads to a better one.
Nobody takes that job for its own sake — it's a stepping stone and everyone treats it as one.
job security
noun phrase
/sɪˈkjʊərəti/
Confidence that employment will continue.
My parents' generation traded excitement for job security, and on balance I think they got the better deal.
burn out
phrasal verb
/bɜːn ˈaʊt/
Become exhausted by sustained overwork.
People burn out not because the hours are long but because nothing they do ever feels finished.
the bottom line
idiom
/ˈbɒtəm laɪn/
The decisive consideration.
The bottom line is that people stay where they feel respected, regardless of what they're paid.
punch above your weight
idiom
/pʌntʃ əˈbʌv/
Perform beyond what your size or resources suggest.
Small firms often punch above their weight precisely because they can decide things in an afternoon.
put in the hours
collocation
/pʊt ɪn ði ˈaʊəz/
Do the sustained work required.
Talent gets you noticed; putting in the hours is what keeps you there.

grammar.intro: Part 3 grammar has one job: to carry reasoning. These five structures are the ones that do argumentative work rather than decorative work, and the six error patterns below are the ones that most often undermine an otherwise strong discussion answer.

structures.form: must / is likely to / may well / would probably / tends to
structures.ex: That may well be the case, though it tends to break down in smaller towns.
structures.note: May well is stronger than may. Tends to is the most useful hedging verb in English and nobody uses it enough.

structures.form: Although / while / even though + clause · or fronted: Granted, …
structures.ex: While awareness has clearly improved, behaviour has not moved with it.
structures.note: Fronting the concession before your own claim is what signals that you considered the other side rather than ignored it.

structures.use: Foregrounding the real point of your answer.
structures.form: What matters is …  ·  It isn't X that …, it's Y
structures.ex: It isn't the amount of choice that paralyses people, it's the fear of choosing wrongly.
structures.note: The single most efficient reframing structure in the language. One cleft per Part 3 is worth planning for.

structures.form: Provided that / as long as / unless + clause
structures.ex: Provided there's a cheap alternative, a levy works. Unless there is, you're simply taxing poverty.
structures.note: The conditional close is the Band 8 ending. It delivers a complex structure and an intellectually honest verdict at once.

structures.form: be + past participle, agent often omitted
structures.ex: Awareness campaigns are launched months before the decision is actually made.
structures.note: Useful when the actor is obvious or irrelevant. Overused it sounds evasive, so one or two instances only.

errors.bad: <s>Although</s> technology is useful, <s>but</s> it also has many disadvantages.
errors.good: Although technology is useful, it also has real disadvantages.
errors.why: One conjunction per relationship. This transfers directly from Vietnamese and is one of the most recognisable markers of a Vietnamese speaker's English.

errors.n: Agreement with collective and indefinite subjects
errors.bad: <s>People is</s> more careful nowadays. / <s>Everyone have</s> their own opinion.
errors.good: People are more careful nowadays. / Everyone has their own opinion.
errors.why: People is plural; everyone, everybody, nobody take singular verbs despite plural meaning. Both appear constantly in Part 3.

errors.bad: In the future, everyone <s>will work</s> from home and offices <s>will disappear</s>.
errors.good: In all likelihood more people will work from home, though I doubt offices disappear entirely.
errors.why: Not grammatically wrong, but unhedged certainty about the future reads as unreflective and forfeits the modal range the question is offering.

errors.bad: It is <s>more easier</s> now. / This is <s>the most important</s> than the others.
errors.good: It is much easier now. / This is more important than the others.
errors.why: Never double-mark a comparative, and never use a superlative with than. Both errors are basic and both are heard frequently at Band 6 to 7.

errors.bad: It <s>depends of</s> the situation. / We should <s>discuss about</s> the causes. / I'm <s>concerned for</s> privacy.
errors.good: It depends on the situation. / We should discuss the causes. / I'm concerned about privacy.
errors.why: These recur so reliably that examiners hear them as a set. Learning the three together takes ten minutes and removes a persistent basic error.

errors.bad: People <s>which</s> live in cities… / The policy <s>who</s> was introduced…
errors.good: People who live in cities… / The policy that was introduced…
errors.why: Who for people, which or that for things. Also note that a non-defining clause requires a comma and cannot use that.

models.html: I think there are some reasons. First, some people are afraid of making a mistake. They worry that if they choose wrong, they will regret it later. Second, nowadays we have too many choices so it is difficult to decide. Also, some people don't have enough experience so they don't know what is the best. So I think these are the main reasons.

notes.fc: Clear and organised, with sequencing markers. But the markers are the most basic set available (First, Second, Also, So) and they are used to list rather than to reason. The three reasons sit in parallel with no relationship between them.
notes.lr: Afraid of making a mistake, too many choices, not enough experience. Adequate and accurate; nothing is less common and nothing is imprecise.
notes.gr: Present simple with subordinate clauses. One error: what is the best should be what the best option is — an embedded question with the word order of a direct one. Meaning survives, which is Band 6.
notes.pr: Intelligible with appropriate chunking, but the three reasons are delivered with identical intonation, so the listener hears a list rather than an argument.

models.html:
The obvious answer is fear of getting it wrong, and that's clearly part of it. But I suspect the bigger factor is that we simply have far more options than previous generations did.

My parents chose between two or three careers that were realistically open to them. I had something like forty, most of which I knew nothing about. And counter-intuitively, more choice tends to make people less decisive, not more — because every option you take now has thirty-nine visible alternatives attached to it.

So I'd say fear is the symptom. The abundance of choice is the cause.

notes.fc: The answer moves rather than lists: obvious reason dispatched, better reason developed, then the two are ranked against each other. Markers do different jobs (but I suspect, and counter-intuitively, so I'd say) rather than sequencing.
notes.lr: Counter-intuitively, less decisive not more, the abundance of choice. Less common items used accurately, and the concrete generational comparison supplies precision that abstract vocabulary alone would not.
notes.gr: A comparative with far, a non-defining relative (most of which), and a causal subordinate clause. Error-free and flexibly varied.
notes.pr: The final two sentences are parallel and short, with contrastive stress on symptom and cause. That pairing is what makes the ranking audible rather than merely stated.

models.html:
Fear of being wrong is the usual answer, and it's true as far as it goes — but it doesn't explain why the difficulty has got worse rather than better. People a century ago made decisions with far less information and considerably more confidence.

What's changed, I think, is that choice has expanded faster than our capacity to evaluate it. My grandmother chose between farming and marrying; I chose between roughly forty career paths, thirty-five of which I couldn't have described. More options, but no better equipment for judging them.

And there's a second thing underneath that — we've started treating decisions as statements about who we are rather than as bets about what might work. If choosing a job is choosing an identity, then every wrong choice is a small indictment, and of course people hesitate.

So: the volume of choice makes decisions harder to evaluate, and the meaning we attach to them makes them harder to risk. I'd argue the second does considerably more damage than the first.

notes.fc: The answer takes the standard explanation, shows why it is insufficient, supplies two better ones, and ranks them. Four paragraphs with distinct functions and no drift. Pauses are clearly used to select the next idea, not to retrieve a word.
notes.lr: True as far as it goes, expanded faster than our capacity, a small indictment, bets about what might work. Precise, idiomatic, and doing conceptual work — statements about who we are rather than bets about what might work is the distinction the whole answer rests on.
notes.gr: A fronted concessive, a relative clause with a quantifier (thirty-five of which), a first conditional carrying an argument, and a verbless clause used for emphasis. Essentially error-free with structures chosen for rhetorical function.
notes.pr: More options, but no better equipment for judging them is delivered as a single contrastive unit with the weight on equipment. The colon-like pause after So in the final paragraph signals a summary before any words do. Stress and intonation are conveying precise meaning throughout.

diffs: Standard answer challenged → two causes → ranked → verdict
But I suspect, counter-intuitively, so I'd say — functional
True as far as it goes, what's changed, underneath that — argumentative
Comparison plus a reframing of what a decision is
Fronted concessive, quantified relative, argumentative conditional
52 seconds — at the upper limit before interruption
Parallel short closers with contrastive stress
Pace and grouping vary; the summary is signalled phonologically
